q: An outcrop of ancient desert sandstone above the village of Zobing carries some of the finest Riesling in the country. Name the site and its region.
exp: The Heiligenstein is Permian sandstone laid down in a desert some 270 million years ago, shot through with volcanic material, and it is unlike anything around it. Achleiten and Loibenberg are real sites but both sit in the Wachau, and the Spitzerberg is a limestone ridge planted to Blaufrankisch.

q: Downstream of the Wachau the terraces give way to thick loess around a riverside town, with a baroque abbey looking across from the hill opposite. Which region borrows the town's name?
exp: Krems stands where the Wachau ends, and Gottweig Abbey occupies its hill south of the river. The western edge of the region still works primary rock, but loess is what most of it grows on, and loess is what Gruner Veltliner does best.

q: Limestone and conglomerate underlie a small region on a Danube tributary south of Krems, which is unusual company for Gruner Veltliner. Which region?
exp: The Traisen flows north into the Danube, and loess covers most of the valley as it does elsewhere along the river. What sets the region apart is what lies under it: a spine of lime-rich conglomerate, Alpine gravel cemented hard, running the length of the western slope and breaking the surface on the best sites. The wines come out firm and stony, with a chalkier edge than the Danube regions on either side of them.

q: One Lower Austrian region is effectively a single enormous loess terrace north of the Danube, and it is the last stronghold of Roter Veltliner. Which?
exp: The Wagram is a step in the landscape rather than a hill, with loess many metres deep along its face. Roter Veltliner is an old, thick-skinned variety that survives almost nowhere else and gives a broad, nutty, low-acid wine.

q: Rows of low cellar doors line a lane running out of a village north of Vienna, with no houses attached to any of them. What is the lane called?
exp: Press houses and cellars were dug into the loess outside the village, clear of the fire risk and the smell, and they line up into whole streets of them. A Buschenschank is a tavern selling a grower's own wine, a Ried is a single vineyard and a Weinstrasse is a signposted tourist route.

q: Between the Danube and the Czech border lies the country's most extensive stretch of vineyard, on rolling loess, and its name states plainly what it grows. Which region?
exp: Weinviertel means wine quarter; the Waldviertel immediately west of it means forest quarter and grows almost none. This was the region chosen to launch the whole DAC system with the 2002 vintage, on peppery dry Gruner Veltliner.

q: A Roman legionary town on the Danube east of Vienna gave its name to a modern wine region built on red wine. Which region?
exp: Carnuntum was a garrison and then a provincial capital, and its ruins stand among the vineyards at Petronell. Zweigelt leads the plantings at better than a quarter and Blaufrankisch is the other red the DAC is built on, though Gruner Veltliner is the second most planted variety and close to half the region is white. The limestone ridge of the Spitzerberg is its most admired site.

q: Spa towns and hot springs south of Vienna gave a wine region its name, and Gumpoldskirchen is its best-known village. Which region?
exp: Thermen means thermal baths, and Baden bei Wien has been taking the waters since Roman times. The northern half grows Zierfandler and Rotgipfler around Gumpoldskirchen; the southern half turns to Sankt Laurent and Pinot Noir on gravel.

q: Warm dry air pushes west off the Hungarian plain and reaches the vineyards around the Neusiedler See and east of Vienna. What is that influence called?
exp: The Pannonian basin behaves like a small continent: hot summers, cold winters and little rain, which is what lets red grapes ripen this far north. Cold air draining off the wooded hills at night holds the acidity in place, and that daily swing is the making of eastern Austrian wine.

q: White pepper, green lentil, grapefruit and a faintly bitter almond finish turn up again and again in one Austrian variety. Which?
exp: The pepper comes from rotundone, the same compound behind the spice of cool-climate Syrah, and growers call the note Pfefferl. Gruner covers about a third of Austria's vineyard and ranges from a light spritzy carafe wine to something that will hold twenty years.

q: Two Austrian varieties share the Veltliner name, one of them green and one of them red. How are the two related?
opts: They are one variety, picked early for one name and late for the other
Hardly at all, since they are separate varieties that share a name
The green is a crossing of the red with Riesling
The red is a colour mutation of the green, as Pinot Gris is of Pinot Noir
exp: Gruner Veltliner turned out to be a seedling of Traminer and an obscure vine found at St Georgen in Burgenland. Roter Veltliner is a quite different old variety and is itself a parent of Neuburger and Rotgipfler.

q: One high-acid Austrian white borrows Riesling's name without sharing any of its parentage, and appears both as a light Styrian carafe wine and as a great botrytis wine in Burgenland. Which?
exp: Welschriesling is grown right across central Europe under other names and has no relationship whatever to the Rhine grape. Its ferocious acidity is exactly what makes it useful when sugars climb, which is why so much Burgenland Beerenauslese is built on it.

q: A Styrian wine list offers Morillon beside its Sauvignon Blanc. What is the guest actually being sold?
exp: Morillon is the Styrian name for Chardonnay and nothing else, most often made there in a taut unoaked style. Weissburgunder appears on the same lists and is Pinot Blanc under another name, a genuinely different grape from Chardonnay rather than a third synonym for it.

q: Two white varieties, one of them also called Spatrot, grow almost nowhere outside the hills south of Vienna and are frequently blended with one another. Which pair?
exp: Zierfandler, or Spatrot, brings acidity and Rotgipfler brings weight and a spicy perfume, and Gumpoldskirchen built its name on the combination. Zierfandler has nothing to do with Zinfandel despite the look of the word, and Blauburger is a red grape.

q: Set an Austrian Riesling beside a Mosel Riesling of comparable quality. What is the most reliable difference?
opts: The Austrian will be softer and lower in acidity
The Austrian will be noticeably sweeter and lower in alcohol
The Austrian will have been aged in new oak
The Austrian will be dry and appreciably higher in alcohol
exp: Austria finishes almost all its Riesling dry, and the Wachau and Kamptal ripen it to twelve or thirteen percent on stony terraces. German Riesling covers the whole sweetness range and on the Mosel is frequently under nine percent.

q: A guest wants a light, juicy red with soft tannin, something that will take twenty minutes in the fridge before lunch. Which Austrian variety fits best?
exp: Zweigelt was bred at Klosterneuburg in 1922 by crossing Sankt Laurent with Blaufrankisch, and it inherited the softness of one and the colour of the other. It is the most planted red in the country and the everyday red of the Heuriger.
